texto_en: The 8.0% figure summarises results from hundreds of studies included in previous reviews. It is a pooled prevalence, useful for understanding the order of magnitude of ADHD in children and adolescents, but it is not equivalent to a worldwide administrative diagnostic rate.
Present 8.0% as the pooled prevalence from an umbrella review, with its 95% CI and the size of the evidence base. Do not present it as worldwide registered diagnosis.

It is not a worldwide census or a WHO statistic. It is a pooled estimate from studies using different methods. It should appear as a meta-analysis, not as ‘8% of all children in the world have an ADHD diagnosis’.

An international meta-analysis estimated a 2020 prevalence of 2.58% for adult ADHD persisting from childhood, equivalent to about 139.84 million adults. When a definition of symptomatic adult ADHD was used without requiring proof of childhood onset, the estimate was 6.76%, about 366.33 million. These are different definitions and should not be presented as a single figure.
There are two different figures and they should not be mixed.
Estimate adjusted to the 2020 global demographic structure:
symptomatic adult ADHD, regardless of proof of childhood onset

The meta-analysis builds two estimates because it uses two definitions of adult ADHD. One requires persistence from childhood and the other is based on adult symptoms without requiring proof of that onset; this is why the percentages and resulting millions are different.
Keep the two definitions separate: ADHD persisting from childhood (2.58%) and symptomatic adult ADHD (6.76%). Do not add or average the two figures.
The figure must remain linked to its population, territory, year and method. Separating it from that context can change its meaning.

An international meta-analysis estimated that developmental dyslexia affects approximately 7.1% of primary-school pupils. In the analysed body of evidence, no significant differences were found between alphabetic and logographic writing systems.

The indicator summarises studies of primary-school pupils and allows comparisons, within the meta-analysis, by sex and writing system. It does not automatically describe adult prevalence or guarantee the same rate in every language or country.
Cite 7.10% as a pooled estimate in primary-school pupils. Do not automatically extrapolate it to all ages or to every country.
Heterogeneity was very high and operational definitions varied between studies. It is a scientific estimate, not a worldwide administrative register.

A systematic review and meta-analysis published in 2024 estimated a pooled prevalence of 5% for developmental coordination disorder in the general child population. Variation between studies was high, so the figure should be read as a scientific synthesis and not as an identical rate for all countries.
